case_title: Santosh S/O Shankar Pawar v. State of Maharashtra
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor (the judgment states the couple lived in poverty)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (FIR initially registered under s.307 IPC, later altered to s.302)
weapon: Kerosene poured from a lamp, and a lighted matchstick thrown on the victim
evidence_type: Dying declaration; oral eyewitness-type testimony of family members (PW2, PW3); medical evidence (post-mortem, doctor's fitness certificate); panch witness evidence on kerosene lamp
aggravating_circumstances: Death within three months of marriage (bride burning); suspicion of infidelity; no provocation for pouring kerosene; victim set ablaze
mitigating_circumstances: None noted by the court; the defence's claims (no premeditation, attempt to extinguish fire, own burns) were rejected
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC s.302; life imprisonment and fine of Rs.1000 (default two months rigorous imprisonment)
high_court_outcome: Appeal dismissed; conviction and sentence upheld
neutral_facts: The victim had been married to the accused only a short time before the incident, and the couple lived in a rented house near the victim's parental home. Both earned a living through daily wage work. On the morning of the incident, the victim went out to answer a call of nature and, on returning somewhat late, was questioned by the accused, who suspected her of infidelity. Despite her attempts to explain, the accused began assaulting her with fists and kicks. He then poured kerosene from a nearby lamp over her and set her ablaze. Her saree caught fire and she ran towards the accused, whose hands were burnt. When she screamed for help, the accused poured water on her. Neighbours and her parents gathered and she was taken to hospital. On the way, she told her mother, sister-in-law and a neighbour what had happened. The neighbour testified only that she said the accused had beaten and kicked her, and did not support the account of kerosene. A sub-inspector recorded her statement at the hospital, on which a First Information Report was registered. After a doctor certified her mental fitness, an executive magistrate recorded a dying declaration naming the accused as the person who poured kerosene and set her on fire. She succumbed to burn injuries on 12 September 2005. The post-mortem found death due to shock and septicaemia caused by 60% burn injuries. A panch witness spoke to a kerosene lamp prepared in an empty liquor bottle in the house. The accused's defence was that the fire was accidental and that he had tried to extinguish it.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from shock and septicaemia due to 60% burn injuries; accused's hands also burnt
premeditation_planning: No premeditation or planning found; court held absence of premeditation did not reduce the offence, given the clear act of setting the victim ablaze
motive: Suspicion of the victim's infidelity after she returned late from answering nature's call
key_evidence_accepted: Dying declaration (Ex.1) recorded by the executive magistrate after doctor's fitness certificate (PW6); oral evidence of PW2 (mother) and PW3 (sister-in-law); post-mortem evidence (PW8)
witness_credibility: PW2 and PW3 found reliable and corroborative; PW1 did not support the kerosene account, but the court still accepted the dying declaration and family testimony as not to be doubted
post_offence_conduct: Accused poured water on the victim only when she screamed; court viewed this as an attempt to cloak guilt, not as remorse
trial_duration: offence: 4.9.2005; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 02.02.2012; Supreme Court: 21.04.2015
legal_representation: Accused/appellant: Shashi Bhushan Kumar. State/respondent: Sushil Kranjkar, Dharmendra Kishor, Aniruddha P. Mayee
investigation_status: FIR registered on victim's statement (s.307); altered to s.302 on death; autopsy, inquest and chargesheet completed; trial held
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under s.302, life imprisonment and fine Rs.1000. High Court: appeal dismissed, conviction and sentence confirmed. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed (SLP notice limited to nature of offence)
prosecution_argument: Pouring kerosene and throwing a lighted matchstick showed intention to cause death; conviction under s.302 was correct
defence_argument: Fire was accidental; accused rushed to extinguish it and was burnt; no premeditation or intent to kill; relied on Kalu Ram to reduce the offence
legal_principle_applied: Intention to kill distinguishes murder from culpable homicide; absence of premeditation does not reduce murder where the act of setting ablaze is clear; clause (iv) of s.300; concurrent findings not disturbed unless perverse
precedent_relied_upon: Kalu Ram v. State of Rajasthan (2000) 10 SCC 324 (held inapplicable); Satya Narayan Tiwari v. State of UP (2010) 13 SCC 689 (referred); Dhananjay Shanker Shetty v. State of Maharashtra (2002) 6 SCC 596 (referred)
sentencing_rationale: Bride burning cases require stern treatment and the maximum penalty prescribed by law to deter others
judicial_aggravating_factors: No provocation; deliberate setting of victim ablaze; death within three months of marriage (bride burning); accused in full senses; water poured only as an attempt to cloak guilt
